pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 8–9 years

- **Topic:** Will the bulb light up?

- **Standards — UK (DfE National Curriculum, KS2 Year 4 Electricity, statutory):** 'identify whether or not a lamp will light in a simple series circuit, based on whether or not the lamp is part of a complete loop with a battery.'

- **Standards — US (NGSS):** National (NGSS): no direct grade-3/4 performance expectation; nearest strand 4-PS3-2 is foreshadowed only. UK-anchored.

- **Operational details:** Children predict and check whether a lamp will light, on the basis of whether the circuit forms a complete, unbroken loop. The reasoning is qualitative and visual (is the path closed? is anything broken or loose?), not about current magnitude. This is the conceptual pivot of Year-4 electricity: the COMPLETE LOOP rule, applied as a predict-then-test judgement and as fault-finding when a build doesn't work.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier A (concrete/observational, age 8-9).
bestPractices: Use predict-then-test relentlessly: show a circuit, ask 'will it light?', have children commit, then close the circuit to check — the gap between prediction and result is where the loop rule is learned.
Build a bank of near-identical circuits differing by ONE feature (a gap, a clip on insulation, a flat cell, a bulb not in its holder, an extra bulb) so children isolate what breaks the loop.
Teach finger-tracing the loop as the diagnostic move: follow the path from one terminal back to the other; if you can't get all the way round, it won't light.
Frame failures as fault-finding, not mistakes: 'it didn't light — where is the break?' turns every dark bulb into a diagnosis task.
Keep it qualitative — lights / doesn't light — and resist 'brighter/dimmer' reasoning, which belongs to later years; the standard is binary.
keyRepresentations: Matched pairs of circuit diagrams — one complete, one with a single break — for 'will it light?' judgements.
The finger-trace loop overlay used as a fault-finding tool.
A close-up gallery of common breaks: gap in a wire, crocodile clip on plastic, bulb loose in holder, reversed/flat cell.
A green-loop / red-break visual code showing the path either closing or stopping at the fault.
commonMisconceptions: Current-used-up / attenuation: thinking the bulb 'uses up' the electricity so the return wire is unnecessary — leads to accepting an incomplete loop.
Unipolar model: one connection to the bulb should be enough to light it.
Believing a bulb merely touching the battery will light without a full path through both its contacts.
Thinking a visible, tidy-looking circuit must work — not checking that every join actually conducts (clip on bare metal, bulb seated).
Assuming more cells or more wire guarantees lighting regardless of whether the loop is complete.

learn.summary: For 8–9 year olds judging whether a lamp lights in a simple series circuit: the core rule is that a bulb lights only when it sits in a complete, unbroken loop from one terminal of a working cell, through the bulb (both its contacts) and back to the other terminal, with any switch closed. Learners commit to a prediction (lights / won't light), then test, then trace the loop to locate any break. The reasoning is qualitative (is the path closed?), never about current magnitude or brightness. Activities move from live predict-test-repair work to scored sorting of circuit pictures to annotated fault-finding references, with explicit attention to the unipolar, 'used-up current', and 'touching is enough' misconceptions.

activities.title: Will it light? Predict, test, then trace the break
feedback: On a wrong 'will light' call, show the traced path stopping at the break so the learner sees precisely where the loop fails, then name the fault (e.g. 'the clip is on the plastic, not the metal').
When a repair succeeds, confirm that closing the one break completed the loop end-to-end, so the bulb now lights.
If the learner judges by distance from the battery, point out that the same single loop feeds the bulb wherever it sits, so distance does not decide lighting.
activities.rationale: Predict-then-test makes the gap between expectation and result the place where the loop rule is learned; single-variable variation lets the learner attribute the result to one cause; repairing and re-testing turns a dark bulb into a diagnosis task rather than a failure. A live model can show the stopping point of the path, but a finger-trace on paper or on real apparatus achieves the same diagnostic move.
sourceClaims: Current-used-up/attenuation and unipolar models lead children to accept incomplete loops; predict-then-test and tracing the complete loop are effective remedies.
Year 4 statutory requirement: identify whether or not a lamp will light based on whether it is part of a complete loop with a battery.
learnerActions: Look at a circuit and commit out loud (or on paper) to 'will light' or 'won't light' BEFORE anything is powered.
Power the circuit (close the switch, or run a screen model) and compare the result to your prediction.
When a prediction is wrong, trace the loop: follow the path with a finger (or watch a moving dot/marker) from one battery terminal all the way round — note exactly where it stops.
In a repair step, fix the fault you found (close the gap, reseat a loose bulb, move a clip off the plastic coating, or re-route a wire to the correct terminal) and re-test.

Work through a sequence of near-identical circuits where each one differs from the last by a single feature (a gap, a clip on insulation, a flat cell, a bulb not seated in its holder, an extra bulb added into the same loop — use bulbs and a cell matched so that both bulbs visibly light).
activities.intendedInsight: A bulb lights when it is part of a complete, unbroken loop from one terminal of a WORKING cell, through the bulb (both its contacts), and back to the other terminal (switch closed). Any single break in the path stops the whole loop; separately, a flat (discharged) cell leaves the loop complete but cannot drive enough current to light the bulb, so that bulb also stays dark. Isolating one variable at a time reveals that, with a working cell strong enough for the bulbs used, loop completeness decides every case in this sequence.

activities.title: Sort the circuits: lights vs won't light
feedback: For each sorted circuit, confirm or correct the placement and name the deciding feature (the completed loop, the exact break, or the flat cell).
If a single-wire or same-terminal picture is placed in 'lights', prompt the learner to trace for a RETURN path to the other terminal before deciding.
activities.rationale: A scored sorting bank cleanly matches the binary standard and can check that the rule generalises across many pictures. Its limit is that the learner cannot repair-and-retest, so it assesses whether the rule is applied but does not itself build the predict-test reflex; pair it with the live predict-test-repair work above. Keep illustrations visually unambiguous rather than relying on fine wiring detail.
sourceClaims: Year 4 statutory requirement: identify whether or not a lamp will light based on whether it is part of a complete loop with a battery.
learnerActions: Given a set of clear, unambiguous circuit pictures, decide for each whether the bulb lights and place it in a 'lights' or 'won't light' group.
For each 'won't light' picture, name the fault (gap in a wire, clip on insulation, loose bulb, open switch, both wires on the same terminal, or a flat cell).
Justify at least one judgement by describing the full loop you traced (or the point where the trace stopped).
activities.intendedInsight: The judgement is binary — lights or does not — and depends on whether an unbroken loop exists with a working cell. Naming the specific fault for each non-working circuit reinforces that a path break can sit anywhere in the loop, while a flat cell fails for a different reason (no working energy source).

activities.title: Fault-finding reference: where is the fault, and why does the bulb stay dark?
feedback: When a fault is revealed, confirm the explanation links it to the cause (a broken path, or a dead cell) rather than just 'it's wrong'.
If a learner assumes a neat circuit must work, highlight an example where a clip sits on insulation or a bulb is unseated so the join does not conduct.
activities.rationale: A tap-to-reveal annotated reference supports the language of fault-finding and the 'check that every join actually conducts' habit. On its own it does not deliver the predict→test cycle, so it works best as a companion to hands-on or live-model practice.
learnerActions: On a single annotated circuit, reveal each marked fault in turn (gap in a wire, crocodile clip on plastic, bulb loose in its holder, flat cell).

For each revealed fault, state in your own words why it stops the bulb lighting — a break means no complete path, while a flat cell means the loop is complete but the cell cannot drive enough current to light the bulb.

Build a checklist of what to check, in order, when a real circuit won't light (e.g. is every join on bare metal? is the bulb seated? is the switch closed? is the cell flat? is there a return path to the other terminal?).
activities.intendedInsight: Fault-finding vocabulary: a tidy-looking circuit can still fail if any single join does not conduct, or if the cell is flat. Learners build a systematic diagnostic routine rather than guessing.

activities.title: Counterexample probe: both wires on the same terminal
feedback: If the learner predicts the same-terminal circuit lights, trace with them from a terminal and show the path never reaches the other terminal — no return, no loop.
When the re-route lights the bulb, confirm that moving one wire created the missing return path and completed the loop.
activities.rationale: This targets the unipolar and 'touching = works' misconceptions directly by forcing a prediction on a circuit that looks connected but has no return path. The reveal-then-repair structure shows the exact feature that decides the outcome.
sourceClaims: Current-used-up/attenuation and unipolar models lead children to accept incomplete loops; predict-then-test and tracing the complete loop are effective remedies.
learnerActions: Examine a circuit where both wires from the bulb go to the SAME battery terminal, so it looks fully connected.
Predict whether the bulb lights and give a reason.
Test (or reveal the result): it stays dark. Then re-route one wire to the OTHER terminal and observe it light.
Explain, by tracing, why the same-terminal version has no return path and so no complete loop.
activities.intendedInsight: 'Connected to the battery' is not the same as 'forms an unbroken loop back to the other terminal'. A bulb needs a full path through BOTH its contacts; one connection, or both wires on one terminal, will not light it.

constraints: Keep the standard binary: judge lights / doesn't light only. Do not introduce brighter/dimmer reasoning, which belongs to later study.

The rule is qualitative and topological (is the path closed?), not about current magnitude. Correct the idea that current is 'used up' along the way: in a single series loop the current is the same all around and is not consumed, so lighting does not depend on distance from the cell.
A complete loop must pass through BOTH contacts of the bulb and return to the other battery terminal; one connection, or both wires on the same terminal, does not light the bulb.

A break anywhere in the path (gap, open switch, clip on insulation, unseated bulb) breaks the whole loop and the bulb stays dark; a tidy-looking circuit can still fail if any join does not conduct. A flat (discharged) cell is a DIFFERENT kind of fault: the loop can be complete but the cell can no longer drive enough current to light the bulb, so distinguish 'no complete path' from 'no working energy source'. Note: a merely reversed but healthy cell still lights a non-polar (filament) bulb in a simple single-cell loop, so do not present reversed polarity as a won't-light fault — only a flat cell reliably prevents lighting.

Sorting or multiple-choice picture tasks check whether the learner can apply the rule but do not let them repair-and-retest; they assess application rather than build the predict-test reflex, so pair them with hands-on or live-model practice.
An annotated static circuit supports fault-finding vocabulary but does not provide the predict→test cycle; use it as a companion, not a replacement.
A screen model of a circuit is a representation of real apparatus; where possible connect it to real bulbs, cells, wires and clips so learners meet real conducting joins.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The IOP Spark misconceptions source is recorded as unverified in the source row; claims that predict-then-test and loop-tracing are 'effective remedies' should be treated as informed practice, not established comparative efficacy.

The original research asserted that a live/2D interactive builds the rule 'faster than any static medium' and that other formats 'can't' teach the predict-test cycle; these comparative/necessity claims are not established by the sources and have been softened to affordance-and-limit statements.

Battery polarity: the source listed 'reversed/flat cell' together as a single fault, but a reversed healthy cell still allows a non-polar lamp to light in a simple single-cell loop. Learner-facing activities and the constraint name only a FLAT (discharged) cell as the fault; review before ever presenting a reversed healthy cell as a 'won't light' case.

Flat cell framing: a flat cell leaves the loop topologically complete but unpowered, so it is not strictly a 'break' in the loop. The intended insight, sort-fault list and constraint have been corrected to distinguish a path break from a dead energy source; the pure 'complete loop → light' rule is now qualified to a working cell.
The source row's reteach pointer for the 'used-up current' misconception is null; a prerequisite reteach step may need to be identified during review.

assess.poeTask: Lay out a circuit where both wires from the bulb go to the SAME battery terminal, so it looks fully connected. Ask the child to predict — will the bulb light? Why? The complete-loop child says no (there's no return path); the 'touching' child says yes. Then reveal it stays dark, and re-route one wire to the other terminal to light it.
probeDeeper: Trace this circuit with your finger from one end of the battery. Does the path get all the way back to the other end?
This circuit has an open switch. The bulb is still wired to the battery — why doesn't it light?
Counterexample: both wires go to the SAME battery terminal. It looks connected — will it light? Why not?
If you found a real circuit that wouldn't light, what would you check first, second, third?
assess.correctAnswer: The bulb lights only when there's a complete, unbroken loop from one terminal of the cell, through the bulb, back to the other terminal, with the switch closed. Any gap — a break, an open switch, or both wires on the same terminal (no return path) — means no complete loop, so the bulb stays off. You tell by tracing the loop with your finger.

errorPatterns.pattern: It lights as long as a wire reaches the bulb from the battery — one path is enough ('electricity goes to the bulb') — the unipolar model.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Trace for a RETURN path to the other terminal; no loop, no light.
errorPatterns.distractor: Yes — the wire carries electricity from the battery to the bulb, so it lights.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Predicts that the same-terminal or single-wire picture will light.

errorPatterns.pattern: Current gets 'used up' on the way, so a bulb closer to the battery lights but a far one doesn't ('the electricity runs low').
errorPatterns.nextMove: The current is the same all around a series loop and isn't consumed — trace that the same loop feeds any bulb in it.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Judges lighting by distance from the cell rather than by loop completeness.

errorPatterns.pattern: A gap or open switch doesn't matter as long as the bulb still touches a wire ('it's still connected').
errorPatterns.nextMove: A gap anywhere breaks the whole loop — the entire path must be unbroken; demonstrate by opening and closing the switch.
errorPatterns.distractor: Yes — the bulb is still joined to the battery by a wire, so the gap doesn't stop it.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says the circuit with an open switch or a small gap will still light.

responseLevels.gap: Predicts lighting from a single connection or 'touching the battery'; ignores whether the loop returns to the other terminal or whether a gap breaks it.
responseLevels.full: Judges every case by tracing an unbroken loop from terminal to terminal through the bulb (switch closed), rejects any circuit lacking a return path, and locates the fault in a non-working one.
responseLevels.partial: Knows a complete loop is needed and spots an obvious break, but is caught out by a same-terminal circuit, an open switch, or 'used-up current' reasoning.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here are four circuit pictures: one complete loop, one with a gap in a wire, one where both wires from the bulb go to the SAME battery terminal, and one with an open switch. For each, will the bulb light? How can you tell just by looking, without building it?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child with the unipolar or 'touching = works' model says a single-wire or same-terminal circuit lights; the complete-loop child rejects any circuit without a full return path. The reason tier separates 'it's connected to the battery' from 'it forms an unbroken loop back to the other terminal'.
